Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. They handled all the small SMD parts well, and the board arrived well soldered and very clean. carswithjoysticks 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. Our customer service ready for your PCB +86-571-85317532 Electric Usagi My aim was to create a simple (no vacuum tube version) of the Usagi Electric bunny for my own personal use, PCBWay reviewed my initial order and provided important feedback so I could revise the order to achieve my ultimate goal. I appreciate the exceptional effort by the PCBWay team. My order was produced quickly and delivered quickly. The quality of the boards is excellent! This project met all of my expectations and I will be happy to order from PCBWay again, in the future. This review is for the electronic board, mounted above the electronic board is a UV printed decorative board with the usagi face, mitchell Bruce Fleming Received boards were 100% Functional Fleming 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. They handled all the small SMD parts well, and the board arrived well soldered and very clean. carswithjoysticks 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
